sections.title: The login at two in the morning
The doors that would have held

narration: Say it is two in the morning.
beats.visual_intent: Night, one key light on a lone work login screen in a dark office; the field fills, the screen answers 'Login successful'; slow push in. Dana seen asleep at home in silhouette, a cut away.

grounding.claim: A fictional employee's account is logged into at night with her real password

beats.delivery: low and unhurried; a beat of quiet before the question

narration: Follow that one password through the night,
and the two habits that stop it.
beats.visual_intent: The password becomes a physical object, a small lit key card, lifted out of the screen into the dark; the camera follows it toward a long corridor of closed doors.

grounding.claim: The attacker used a valid password rather than forcing entry
Two habits stop it: a unique password and MFA
MFA stops a stolen password being enough

narration: Months ago, Dana used one password twice.
beats.visual_intent: Rewind: daylight dimmed to evening; the same key card fits two doors side by side, one labelled Shop, one labelled Work. Plain, no blame.

grounding.claim: Dana reused one password on a shopping site and at work

narration: Then the shopping site is breached.
The password lands in a list.
beats.visual_intent: The Shop door is forced in shadow off to the side; the key card is copied onto a long sheet of other cards, a list that slides from hand to hand in silhouette. The Work door stays in the dark, untouched.

grounding.claim: Passwords leak when a third-party site is breached, outside the employer's control
Leaked credentials are compiled into lists that are shared or traded

beats.misconception: a leak on an unrelated site only costs that one account

narration: Software tries every leaked pair on other logins.
beats.visual_intent: A machine-steady stream of key cards tried against a row of login doors, one after another, automated and indifferent; the term appears once as the stream runs.

grounding.claim: Credential stuffing is automated trying of leaked pairs on other logins
Because it is automated, a reused password does not need to be targeted by a person

beats.misconception: nobody would bother targeting my password

beats.visual_intent: In the stream, Dana's card reaches the Work door and turns; the door opens a crack and light spills out. Hold on the open door.

grounding.claim: Credential stuffing works because the same password is reused on more than one service

narration: Inside, the attacker looks like Dana.
A valid login can be harder to notice.
beats.visual_intent: Inside the office at night, a silhouette at a desk is indistinguishable from an ordinary user; the security camera's view shows nothing unusual.

grounding.claim: A valid account login can look like a normal user and be harder to notice than a forced break-in

narration: From one account, they reach other systems.
They may hunt for more access.
beats.visual_intent: From the first open door, a corridor: one door after another opens in sequence down the line, the light spreading; a last heavier door at the end is tried.

grounding.claim: From one compromised account an attacker uses the foothold to reach other systems and accounts
The attacker may look for higher-privilege accounts

narration: So which habit shuts which door?
beats.visual_intent: Wide on the corridor of open doors, then the two places the night could have stopped are marked: the first login door, and the moment a correct password is used by someone else. Hold for the viewer to choose.

grounding.claim: One reused password led to many systems

recall.answer: a unique password keeps the leaked one from fitting; MFA makes a correct password alone not enough
recall.tempting_wrong: change the password every few months

narration: First, a unique password for every account.
Then a leak opens only that site.
A password manager creates and remembers them.
beats.visual_intent: Replay the leak with two different key cards: the Shop card is copied, tried at the Work door, and does not turn. A small password manager vault hands out a fresh card per door.

grounding.claim: A different password per account means a leak from one service does not unlock the others
A password manager generates and stores unique passwords

beats.misconception: a complex password is safe even if reused

narration: A stolen password alone is not enough.
beats.visual_intent: The stolen card turns in the lock, but a second lock below it stays shut, waiting for a code on Dana's phone. The door holds.

grounding.claim: MFA asks for something beyond the password, so a stolen correct password alone is not enough

narration: But an attacker may send approval requests,
beats.visual_intent: On a bedside phone in the dark, approval requests light up one after another; the thumb presses Deny. The second lock stays shut.

grounding.claim: In MFA fatigue an attacker with the password sends repeated approval requests
An MFA request you did not start should be denied and reported

beats.misconception: any approval prompt is safe to accept

recall.prompt: A request you did not start: what do you do?

narration: This week, replace any work password used elsewhere.
Report odd prompts or breach notices straight away.
beats.visual_intent: Morning light edges in: three plain actions appear as objects on Dana's desk, each picked up as it is named: a fresh key card, the phone with MFA on, a report sent to the security team.

grounding.claim: Replace a reused password with a unique one
Turn on MFA
Report unexpected prompts or breach notices to the security team promptly

narration: A request arrives: denied, and reported.
beats.visual_intent: The opening shot again, two in the morning, one key light: the leaked card is tried at the Work door and does not turn, the phone lights once, Deny; the corridor of doors stays dark and shut. Slow pull back.

grounding.claim: With a unique password the leaked one does not unlock the work account
An unstarted request is denied and reported
The replayed night is the same fictional case

beats.delivery: warm and quiet; let the last line land
